heading: Greedy by End Time
body:
To maximize non-overlapping intervals, **sort by end time** and greedily keep intervals that finish earliest.

Why? An interval ending early leaves more room for future intervals. One ending late blocks more opportunities—even if it starts early.

heading: Flip the Question
body:
Don't count removals directly. Instead:
- Find the **max number of intervals you can keep**
- Subtract from total → removals needed

This reframe unlocks the greedy strategy: keep intervals finishing earliest.

label: Crux · Python
code:
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
end = intervals[0][1]
count = 1

for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
    if intervals[i][0] >= end:
        end = intervals[i][1]
        count += 1

return len(intervals) - count

q: Why do we sort intervals by END time rather than START time?
options: Sorting by start time is O(n²) while sorting by end time is O(n log n)
Intervals ending earliest free up the most time for future intervals, maximizing how many we can keep
End times are always smaller than start times, making the sort faster
Sorting by end time automatically handles the edge case of empty arrays
explain: Keeping intervals that end earliest leaves maximum time for future intervals—the greedy insight.
